title: Variable Consideration Under ASC 606
learning_objectives: Identify various forms of variable consideration
Apply the two estimation methods: expected value and most likely amount
Understand and apply the constraint on variable consideration
Account for subsequent changes in variable consideration estimates
Handle specific types: volume discounts, performance bonuses, returns, price concessions

common_question_types: Calculating expected value vs. most likely amount

definition.description: Variable consideration is any amount of consideration in a contract with a customer that can vary due to discounts, rebates, refunds, credits, price concessions, incentives, performance bonuses, penalties, or other similar items.
definition.key_principle: Variable consideration is part of the transaction price (Step 3 of five-step model), but must be estimated and constrained before inclusion.

estimation_methods.overview: Entity must estimate variable consideration using ONE of two methods - whichever better predicts the amount of consideration to which the entity will be entitled.

method_1_expected_value.title: Expected Value Method
method_1_expected_value.description: The sum of probability-weighted amounts in a range of possible consideration amounts.
when_to_use: Large number of contracts with similar characteristics
Range of possible outcomes with varying probabilities
Historical data available to predict probabilities

facts: Customer purchases: Probabilities based on historical patterns
Scenario 1: $100K purchases (30% probability) → No rebate → Revenue $100K
example.conclusion: Include $137,250 in transaction price (subject to constraint)

method_2_most_likely_amount.title: Most Likely Amount Method
method_2_most_likely_amount.description: The single most likely amount in a range of possible consideration amounts (the single most likely outcome of the contract).
when_to_use: Contract has only two possible outcomes (binary)
One outcome is significantly more likely than all others

facts: Entity has 70% probability of completing on time based on experience
analysis: Most likely amount = $5,500,000 (the outcome with highest probability)
example.conclusion: Include $5,500,000 in transaction price (subject to constraint)

method_2_most_likely_amount.note: Most likely amount is NOT a probability-weighted average. It's the single most likely outcome.

method_selection.principle: Use the method that better predicts the amount entity will be entitled to
practical_guidance: Binary/two outcomes → Usually most likely amount
Many possible outcomes → Usually expected value
Limited experience → Most likely amount may be more appropriate
Large portfolio with history → Expected value often better

constraint_on_variable_consideration.principle: Include variable consideration in transaction price ONLY TO THE EXTENT that it is PROBABLE that a significant reversal in the amount of cumulative revenue recognized will NOT occur when the uncertainty is subsequently resolved.
constraint_on_variable_consideration.threshold: Probable means 'likely to occur' - generally interpreted as >75% probability (higher threshold than 'more likely than not' which is >50%)
constraint_on_variable_consideration.objective: Prevent recognition of revenue that may need to be reversed later

factors_increasing_likelihood_of_reversa.factor: Amount is highly susceptible to factors outside entity's influence
examples: Judgment or actions of third parties (e.g., regulators, courts)

factors_increasing_likelihood_of_reversa.factor: Uncertainty not expected to be resolved for a long period of time
factors_increasing_likelihood_of_reversa.explanation: Longer time periods increase uncertainty and reversal risk

factors_increasing_likelihood_of_reversa.factor: Entity's experience with similar contracts is limited
factors_increasing_likelihood_of_reversa.explanation: Lack of historical data increases estimation uncertainty

factors_increasing_likelihood_of_reversa.factor: Entity has a practice of offering price concessions or changing payment terms
factors_increasing_likelihood_of_reversa.explanation: Pattern of modifications suggests variable consideration estimates may not hold

factors_increasing_likelihood_of_reversa.factor: Contract has large number and broad range of possible consideration amounts

application_process.action: Estimate variable consideration using expected value or most likely amount
Assess factors that increase reversal likelihood
Determine: Is it probable (>75% likely) that significant reversal will NOT occur?
If yes, include full estimated amount. If no, include only amount for which significant reversal is not probable (may be zero).

example_constraint_applied.scenario: Pharmaceutical company with contingent milestone payment
facts: Contingent payment: $5M if drug receives regulatory approval
Most likely amount: $15M (approval is most likely)
However: Regulatory approval highly uncertain, outside entity's control, resolution takes 2+ years
constraint_analysis: - May have limited experience with this specific regulatory process
Conclusion: NOT probable that significant reversal would not occur
Constrained amount: Include only $10M base payment in transaction price
Recognize $5M contingent amount only when regulatory approval obtained (uncertainty resolved)

volume_discounts_and_rebates.description: Customer receives discount or rebate if purchases exceed certain threshold

example.scenario: Retailer offers rebate based on annual purchases
example.terms: 5% rebate if customer purchases exceed $1M in calendar year
approach: Use expected value or most likely amount to estimate rebate
example.accounting: Reduce revenue by estimated rebate; accrue rebate liability

performance_bonuses_penalties.description: Entity receives bonus for meeting targets or incurs penalty for failing to meet targets

example.terms: $100K bonus for early completion; $50K penalty for late completion
approach: Apply most likely amount method (typically three outcomes: early, on-time, late)
Apply constraint considering entity's control over timing
If entity has strong track record, may include bonus in transaction price

rights_of_return.description: Customer has right to return product and receive refund
accounting_treatment: Recognize revenue for products not expected to be returned
Recognize refund liability for products expected to be returned (measured at transaction price)
Recognize asset for right to recover products (measured at carrying amount of inventory less expected recovery costs)
Do not recognize revenue for products expected to be returned

journal_entries.scenario: Sell 1,000 units at $100 each; estimate 5% return rate; cost per unit $60

price_concessions.description: Entity's practice of accepting less than stated contract price
price_concessions.key_point: If entity has history or intention of granting price concessions, stated contract price is not transaction price

example.scenario: Software company regularly accepts 80-90% of invoiced amount to maintain customer relationships
accounting: Transaction price is estimated amount entity expects to collect (e.g., 85% of stated price)
This is variable consideration, not bad debt
Bad debt expense not appropriate because collectibility issue affects contract existence (Step 1), not revenue measurement

sales_usage_based_royalties.description: Consideration based on customer's sales or usage
sales_usage_based_royalties.special_rule: Exception for licenses of intellectual property - recognize royalty revenue only when (or as) the later of:
recognition_criteria: Subsequent sale or usage occurs, OR
Performance obligation to which royalty has been allocated is satisfied (or partially satisfied)
sales_usage_based_royalties.rationale: Exception prevents recognizing revenue before customer's sales/usage occurs (which drives the royalty)

example.scenario: License software with 5% royalty on customer's product sales
example.accounting: Recognize royalty revenue as customer makes sales, even if license granted earlier. Track customer's sales each period and recognize 5% as revenue.

subsequent_changes_in_estimates.principle: Reassess estimated variable consideration at end of each reporting period
accounting_for_changes: Allocate change to performance obligations using same allocation method as at contract inception (Step 4)
Recognize change as adjustment to revenue (Step 5):
- For satisfied POs: Adjust revenue in period of change (catch-up)
- For unsatisfied or partially satisfied POs: Adjust revenue prospectively or catch-up depending on timing recognition

example.scenario: Service contract with year-end bonus based on customer satisfaction

timeline.constraint_assessment: Include bonus - entity has strong track record

timeline.new_information: Customer feedback very positive; increase probability to 90%
timeline.revised_transaction_price: $1.1M (no change in most likely amount - still most likely to earn bonus)

timeline.new_information: Service issues arose; probability drops to 40%
timeline.revised_most_likely_amount: $1.0M (now more likely to NOT earn bonus)
timeline.impact: Reduce transaction price by $100K; adjust revenue recognized to date

allocation_of_variable_consideration.general_rule: Allocate variable consideration to all performance obligations based on relative standalone selling prices
allocation_of_variable_consideration.exception: Allocate variable consideration entirely to one or more (but not all) specific performance obligations IF:
exception_criteria: Terms of variable payment relate specifically to entity's efforts to satisfy that performance obligation (or to specific outcome from satisfying that PO)
Allocating variable amount entirely to that PO is consistent with allocation objective when considering all POs and payment terms in contract

example.scenario: Software license + implementation services + ongoing support
example.variable_consideration: Bonus for completing implementation within 30 days
example.analysis: Bonus relates specifically to implementation PO (not to license or support)
example.allocation: Allocate bonus entirely to implementation PO; allocate fixed consideration across all three POs

methodology_selection: Two outcomes or one dominant outcome → Most likely amount
Many outcomes with historical data → Expected value
When in doubt, show both methods and explain why you chose one
constraint_application: Always mention the constraint - even if you conclude it doesn't prevent inclusion
List factors present in the scenario that affect reversal risk
State conclusion clearly: Is significant reversal probable or not probable?
If reversal is probable, either exclude variable consideration or include conservative amount
common_mistakes: Forgetting to apply constraint after calculating estimate
Using probability-weighted average when most likely amount is appropriate
Confusing 'probable' threshold (should NOT reverse, >75%) with 'more likely than not' (>50%)
Treating price concessions as bad debt expense instead of reduction to revenue

key_points: Variable consideration is estimated using expected value or most likely amount
Expected value = probability-weighted; Most likely amount = single most likely outcome
Constraint requires it to be PROBABLE (>75%) that significant reversal will NOT occur
Factors increasing reversal risk: outside entity's influence, long time period, limited experience, broad range of outcomes
Rights of return require refund liability and asset for right to recover
Royalty exception for IP licenses: recognize only when/as customer's sales occur
Variable consideration can be allocated specifically to one PO if criteria met
